claims.text: A short-duration controlled anneal of an as-synthesized single-phase magnetic high-entropy alloy will nucleate fine nanoscale precipitates.
The anneal may induce slight local ordering in the disordered matrix.
Anneal-induced nanoscale precipitates or local ordering will act as effective magnetic-domain-wall pinning centers.
The increased domain-wall pinning will raise coercivity relative to the untreated alloy.
The proposed initial material is an as-synthesized, single-phase, compositionally disordered magnetic high-entropy alloy.
The initial alloy has relatively low coercivity.
An optimized intermediate-temperature, brief anneal can promote nanoprecipitation without causing full-scale phase separation or excessive grain growth.
The intervention is to be performed under a controlled atmosphere while alloy composition is held constant.
Coercivity should be compared between treated and untreated samples at room temperature or another regime in which domain-wall pinning is evident.
The structural mediator is the formation of nanoscale precipitates or slight local ordering within the disordered matrix.
Precipitates increase the local energy barrier to magnetic-domain-wall motion.
Annealed samples will have higher coercive field than the matched as-synthesized baseline.
The increase in coercivity will be caused by enhanced domain-wall pinning from the anneal-induced precipitates.
The coercivity increase is expected only when annealing forms fine precipitates without detrimental phase separation, excessive grain growth, or significant compositional change.
Excessive phase separation, grain growth, or compositional change could negate the proposed pinning benefit.
The annealing temperature, duration, and magnitude of the coercivity increase are not yet known and require systematic optimization.
Magnetic hysteresis measurements can determine whether annealing produces a statistically significant coercivity increase relative to an untreated control.
TEM, SEM, and XRD can be used to assess precipitate formation and unwanted phase changes after annealing.
Failure to observe a statistically significant coercivity increase in the annealed samples would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis is explicitly conditioned on avoiding adverse phase separation and large precipitates, but the falsification rule treats occurrence of those out-of-bound microstructures as falsification. Such a result would show failure to satisfy the stated boundary conditions rather than directly falsify the conditional hypothesis.
